summary: Same fire/spark strip animation with a near-identical palette ramp, same left-to-right advection at within ~20% of the original's speed and a comparable spark cadence, but the port's heat envelope is wrong on a major axis: it is 3-4x cooler than the original on the default 60 px rig, its heat decays 2-4x faster down the strip, and it does not reproduce the original's frame-rate runaway (at the harness default 20 fps the original saturates to a solid, frozen white strip while the port renders a live fire) or its 1/N-style intensity collapse with pixel count.
observations: Both sides compile and run with no compile/runtime errors on every run; neither side exposes ANY control (meta.json controls: [] on orig and port; --probe-controls printed '(no settable controls)' for both). Control surfaces match exactly.
Neither side binds sensors (wantsSensors: false on both), so all runs were sensors: off.

Shared structure (default rig, strip 60 px): a fire waterfall seeded at pixel index 0 with heat streaming toward increasing index and fading out. Palette on both is black -> deep red -> red -> orange -> yellow -> white-hot. Direction, source location and general silhouette match.

PALETTE RAMP MATCHES ALMOST EXACTLY. Bucketing every dumped pixel by its max channel over 60 frames (120 px, 5 fps) gives, for buckets max~8/72/136/200/232/248 - orig rgb = (6,0,0)/(70,0,0)/(133,5,0)/(199,18,0)/(232,28,0)/(254,78,11); port = (9,0,0)/(71,1,0)/(135,7,0)/(199,23,0)/(232,37,0)/(254,100,8). Port is a touch yellower at the top of the ramp (g=100 vs 78 at full red) - a nitpick, not a divergence. The huge blue-channel gap seen in whole-rig stats on the default rig (orig meanB 77.5 vs port 2.5 at 60 px / 5 fps) is entirely a heat-level artefact of the original clipping to white, not a palette difference.

BRIGHTNESS GAP ON THE DEFAULT RIG. 60 px, 60 s @ 5 fps: orig meanBrightness avg 117.7 (min 17, max 184) vs port 34.7 (min 12, max 49) - a 3.4x mean deficit. 60 px, 6 s @ 20 fps (baseline): orig avg 189.9 vs port 129.7. Mean spatial profile over 40 frames at 60 px / 5 fps: orig is CLIPPED at 255 across indices 1-13 and still 237 at index 20, 152 at 30, 61 at 40, 12 at 50; port peaks at 129 (index 1), is 44 at index 20, 19 at 30, 5 at 40, 1 at 50.

DECAY LAW DIFFERS, independent of clipping. On a 120 px rig at 5 fps the two sides have nearly identical mean brightness (orig 28, port 24) and neither clips much, so the normalized profiles are directly comparable. Normalizing each to its index-1 value: index 20 orig 0.59 / port 0.59 (identical); index 40 orig 0.36 / port 0.23; index 60 orig 0.26 / port 0.09; index 80 orig 0.19 / port 0.04; index 100 orig 0.058 / port 0.020. The two agree for the first ~20% of the strip and then the port's tail collapses 2-4x faster. Orig's far field is a slow, near-linear fade reaching 0 right at the strip end; port's is a fast exponential that is effectively dark past ~70% of the strip.

ADVECTION SPEED IS CLOSE. Space-time cross-correlation of per-pixel brightness series over 200 consecutive frames (120 px, 20 fps, --skip 30): orig lag 6 frames for pixels 20->40, 9 for 30->60, 13 for 40->80 (66.7 / 66.7 / 61.5 px/s, i.e. ~0.55 strip/s); port lag 8 / 11 / 13 frames (50.0 / 54.5 / 61.5 px/s, ~0.42-0.51 strip/s). Both propagate strictly toward increasing index. Port is ~10-25% slower. (A 5 fps estimate that suggested a 4x speed gap was aliasing - the orig moves ~13 px per 0.2 s step there - and is not reportable.)

SPARK CADENCE IS CLOSE. Counting local maxima in single-pixel brightness series over 10 s (120 px, 20 fps): orig 1.6-2.4 events/s at pixels 2/10/30/60; port 0.8-1.5 events/s. Port fires roughly 30-40% fewer sparks - visible in the waterfalls as a sparser streak density, but the same order.

FRAME-RATE COUPLING: BOTH SIDES ARE FRAME-STEPPED, BUT THE ORIGINAL RUNS AWAY ~3x SOONER. Mean brightness on 60 px vs fps - orig: 2 fps 57, 3 fps 55, 5 fps 118, 10 fps 216, 20 fps 235, 40 fps 243; port: 2 fps 27, 3 fps 27, 5 fps 35, 10 fps 71, 20 fps 162, 40 fps 239. Both blow out to near-white as fps rises; the fps at which each reaches mean ~200 is ~9 for the orig and ~25 for the port.

DEGENERATE ORIGINAL AT THE HARNESS DEFAULT. 60 px, 180 s @ 20 fps: the original ramps to a completely saturated white strip within ~15 s and then has motion EXACTLY 0.0 in every subsequent 10 s bin (10 s-binned meanBrightness 216 then 255 x 17; motion 7.6 then 0.0 x 17). Over the same window the port is alive and stable (brightness bins 142,182,183,174,...,159; motion bins 5.9-8.0). So at the default rig AND default frame rate the two sides look nothing alike - solid frozen white vs an animated fire - but that is the ORIGINAL being degenerate there, not the port dying.

PIXEL-COUNT SCALING LAWS ARE OPPOSITE. Mean brightness at 5 fps, --skip 30, 20 s, per --pixels: orig 255 (15 px), 255 (30), 139 (60), 27 (120), 11 (240), 4 (480) - i.e. intensity collapses roughly as N^-1.4 once out of clipping. Port: 85 (15), 55 (30), 35 (60), 24 (120), 19 (240), 17 (480) - nearly rig-size independent. Total integrated light DECREASES with N on the original (8340 at 60 px -> 1920 at 480 px) and INCREASES on the port (2100 -> 8160). Consequence: the port is 4x DIMMER than the original at 60 px but 2-4x BRIGHTER at 240-480 px. On a 300 px rig the orig peaks at only ~50 while the port peaks at ~100.

LONG-TIMESCALE BEHAVIOUR DIFFERS. 300 s @ 5 fps, 60 px, 15 s bins - orig meanBrightness 70.6, 117.8, 135.4, 147.1, 129.4, 127.9, 113.4, 134.8, 157.8, 139.0, 124.8, 159.5, 170.6, 166.2, 157.2, 153.0, 140.3, 156.2, 164.5, 144.7 (a ~60 s warm-up ramp then a slow +-20% breathing on a tens-of-seconds timescale); port 33.9, 35.5, 34.7, 34.6, 34.4, 34.3, 35.3, 35.2, 35.1, 34.8, 35.5, 34.4, 34.9, 36.5, 33.4, 34.4, 34.2, 35.1, 34.2, 35.5 (perfectly stationary from t=0, no warm-up, no breathing). The port reaches its steady state instantly and never leaves it.

No mode/regime rotation on either side: the survey rhythm shows one continuous texture for the port, and for the orig only the single warm-up -> volatile-steady transition described above. Regime probes at --skip 0 (mode-warmup) and --skip 200 (mode-steady) confirm - orig 81 -> 153 mean, port 34 -> 35.

SEED-INDEPENDENT STATISTICS on both sides. 60 s @ 5 fps at seeds 1 / 7 / 1234: orig mean 118 / 121 / 118, motion 26 / 24 / 24; port mean 35 / 34 / 34, motion 20 / 19 / 20. The stochastic character is stable, so the brightness/decay gaps above are not a one-seed fluke.

The port is never dead: zeroMotionFrames is 1 (the unavoidable first frame) on every port run including the 3600-frame 180 s one, brightnessTrend steady, no decay to black and no saturation lock. It is the ORIGINAL that freezes (at >=20 fps on 60 px).
feedback: Main fix: the port's fire is too cool and too short-lived on the default 60 px strip. At 5 fps the original's mean brightness is 118 and its core clips at 255 across indices 1-13; the port's mean is 35 and its peak is 129. Roughly 3-4x more heat is needed at the default rig, but see the scaling note below before simply multiplying by a constant - a flat gain would over-brighten the large-rig case.

Second fix: the downstream decay is too fast. Measured on a 120 px rig at 5 fps where neither side clips, normalized to each side's own peak, the original holds 0.36 / 0.26 / 0.19 of peak at indices 40 / 60 / 80 while the port holds 0.23 / 0.09 / 0.04. Both agree up to index ~20 and then the port's tail falls away. The original's far field is a slow, almost linear fade that only reaches zero at the very end of the strip; the port's is a steep exponential that is dark past ~70% of the strip. Lengthen/soften the cooling so a spark's trail survives across the whole strip.

Third fix (structural): the two sides scale oppositely with pixel count. Original mean brightness by --pixels at 5 fps: 255 (15 px), 255 (30), 139 (60), 27 (120), 11 (240), 4 (480) - its total emitted light DROPS as the rig grows. Port: 85, 55, 35, 24, 19, 17 - essentially density-invariant. Whatever the port does per pixel, the original evidently does per fixed budget (spark/heat injection that is not scaled up with pixel count). Matching this law is what makes the 60 px case and the 300 px case agree at the same time.

Fourth (report-only, judgement call for the fixer): the original is frame-rate coupled hard enough that on 60 px at the harness default 20 fps it saturates to a solid white strip within ~15 s and then has motion exactly 0 forever. The port is also frame-coupled but with ~3x more headroom (it needs ~25 fps to reach mean 200 where the original needs ~9). Faithful reproduction would mean reproducing the runaway; if the port is deliberately more fps-tolerant that is arguably an improvement, but it should be a conscious decision and noted, because it is the single biggest reason the two look unrelated at default settings.

Fifth (minor): the original has a ~60 s warm-up ramp (mean brightness 71 in the first 15 s rising to ~150 by 60 s) and then breathes +-20% on a tens-of-seconds timescale; the port is statistically stationary from frame 1 with no warm-up and no slow variation. Adding a slow intensity wander would make the port feel less mechanical.

Sixth (nitpick): the port fires ~30-40% fewer sparks per second (0.8-1.5/s vs the original's 1.6-2.4/s measured at 120 px / 20 fps) and propagates them ~10-25% slower (~0.45 strip/s vs ~0.55 strip/s). Both are close enough that they are not the priority, but nudging the spawn rate up slightly would help the density gap alongside the brightness fix.

Do NOT touch the palette. The colour ramp is essentially exact - bucketed by intensity the two sides' mean RGB agree within a few counts all the way up (orig (133,5,0) vs port (135,7,0) at max~136). The only difference is a slightly yellower white-hot top end on the port (g=100 vs 78 at r=254), which is a rounding-level nitpick.
Neither side has any controls, so there is nothing to add or remove on the control surface.
